cevap: It's really good to hear that "I don't drink in the evenings anymore" — that's a real change you're holding onto. Feeling strange inside makes sense too; new patterns can feel unfamiliar before they feel comfortable. Be patient with yourself as things settle.

It sounds like something good happened — your brother called, and hearing your mother "said the same thing too" must mean a lot. When people who love you start saying similar things, it often means they're noticing you. How did it feel to hear that from both of them?
Going to work and "coming home regularly too" is a steady rhythm, and steady rhythms are worth a lot even when they don't feel dramatic. That kind of consistency adds up. Keep noticing it.
Quitting smoking is a big step on its own, and cutting down on coffee "too" shows you're paying attention to your whole routine. That's a lot to take on at once — be proud of yourself for it.

It sounds painful to sit with your wife's anger and notice the kids "keep away from me too." That kind of distance hurts, but it doesn't have to be permanent. Trust often comes back slowly, in small moments rather than all at once.

Having "no money" and not being able to find a job at the same time is a heavy load to carry. That kind of pressure is real and exhausting. You don't have to solve all of it today — one step is enough for now.

Going to the doctor and staying "regularly" with your routine shows real follow-through in taking care of yourself. That consistency matters, even on days it doesn't feel like much. Keep going at your own pace.

Not being able to sleep, with your appetite "gone too," sounds exhausting on top of everything else. That's a lot for your body and mind to carry right now. Be gentle with yourself through this stretch — it won't always feel this heavy.

It sounds lonely — your friends "don't call," and you notice yourself not calling them either. That pull toward distance is common, but it doesn't mean the connection is gone. Whenever you're ready, even a small hello to one person could feel like a start.

That sounds like a genuinely hard stretch — a bad day, and then "the next day I also couldn't get up." Days like that don't erase the progress you've already made. They're just part of the road, not the whole story.

Carrying something this big alone, not even telling your wife, sounds heavy — "I didn't tell anyone I quit" is a lot to hold by yourself. Whenever it feels right, you get to choose the moment. There's no rush.
A walk in the morning, and "I'll go in the evening too" — that's a lovely rhythm you're building into your day. Moving your body like that can be such a steady, grounding habit. Keep it up.
